title: Builder Pattern
oneLiner: Assembles a complex object step by step, so construction logic doesn't live in one overloaded constructor.

hero.name: The Architect
hero.catchphrase: Step by step, exactly to spec.
hero.power: Assembles complex objects piece by piece through a clear, fluent sequence of steps.
hero.weakness: For a simple object with two or three fields, The Architect is pure ceremony — a plain constructor is faster.
hero.origin: The Architect emerged from a `new HttpRequest(url, null, null, true, false, null, 3000, null, "GET", null)` call that nobody could read six months later.

story.problem: HttpRequest has a 10-argument constructor. Every call site is a wall of positional booleans and nulls that nobody can read or safely modify.
story.solution: The Architect replaces the constructor with a chain of named steps: `.method("GET").timeout(3000).header(...)`. Each step is self-explanatory, and only `.build()` produces the final object.
story.result: Call sites read like sentences. Optional fields are simply skipped instead of passed as null, and the object can't exist half-configured.

before: Optional fields forced into every call as null
Easy to swap two positional arguments by mistake
after: Impossible to swap arguments — each step is named

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A ten-argument constructor call stretches across the screen, half of it null.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Is the 7th argument the timeout or the retry count? I have to open the class to find out. Again.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Architect rolls out a blueprint and starts stacking labeled construction steps.
panels.speaker: The Architect
panels.dialogue: Stop cramming everything into one call. Build it step by step — name every piece as you place it.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: A fluent chain of named methods assembles the request, then .build() seals it.
panels.speaker: The Architect
panels.dialogue: Each step is self-explanatory. Skip what you don't need. Call build() only when it's actually ready.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The new call site reads like plain English, no nulls in sight.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I can read this six months from now without opening the class. That alone was worth it.

useWhen: An object has many optional fields, and most combinations of them are valid.
Construction involves several steps that benefit from being explicit and named.
You want to prevent a half-configured object from ever being used (only `.build()` returns the finished object).
avoidWhen: The object has two or three required fields and no meaningful optional variation — a constructor is simpler.
The 'steps' don't actually need names or ordering — a plain options object achieves the same clarity.
You're building the same object shape every single time with no variation.
commonMistakes: Building a Builder for an object that only ever has one valid configuration — pure overhead.
Forgetting to validate required fields in `.build()`, letting an incomplete object slip through.
Making the builder mutable and reusable in a way that lets one `.build()` call's state leak into the next.
Recreating a full options-object pattern but calling it 'Builder' without the fluent, guided step sequence that makes the pattern worth it.
explanation.realWorldExample: Java's `StringBuilder`, most HTTP client libraries' request builders, and UI component libraries with fluent `.padding().color().onClick()` chains are all Builder in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Couldn't we just use an options object instead — `{ url, method, timeout }`?

conversation.speaker: The Architect
conversation.message: You could, for simple cases. I earn my keep when construction has real steps — validation, defaults, conditional pieces — that benefit from being spelled out and chained.

conversation.speaker: The Architect
conversation.message: When every field is required and there's only one way to build the thing. Then I'm just ceremony — use a constructor.

codeBattle.scenario: Your PDF report generator has a constructor with 12 optional parameters (margins, header, footer, watermark, page size, orientation...), and half of every call site is `null`.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Architect turns those 12 positional nulls into named, optional, chainable steps that only assemble the report once .build() is called.

quiz.question: What problem does Builder primarily solve?
options: Constructors that need many optional parameters become unreadable and error-prone
Two objects need to be kept in sync automatically
A class needs to guarantee only one instance exists
An interface needs to be adapted to another interface
quiz.answer: Constructors that need many optional parameters become unreadable and error-prone
quiz.explanation: Builder replaces a long, positional constructor with clear, named, chainable steps.

quiz.question: What typically finalizes a Builder and returns the constructed object?
options: Automatic construction on the first `.` chain call
A static factory method on the product class
quiz.explanation: The build step is where validation happens and the finished, immutable object is handed back.

quiz.question: When is Builder unnecessary overhead?
options: When the object has few required fields and no meaningful optional variation
When the object has ten or more optional fields
When construction involves several conditional steps
When you want to prevent half-configured objects
quiz.answer: When the object has few required fields and no meaningful optional variation
quiz.explanation: A plain constructor is simpler and clearer when there's nothing complex to guide the caller through.

quiz.question: How does Builder improve on a constructor with many positional boolean/null arguments?
options: Each configuration step is named, so call sites are self-documenting and hard to misuse
It removes the need for any validation
It makes the object mutable forever
It guarantees the object is a singleton
quiz.answer: Each configuration step is named, so call sites are self-documenting and hard to misuse
quiz.explanation: Named, chained steps replace error-prone positional arguments, making intent obvious at the call site.
